question:
A 49-year-old male with a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stable stage 3 chronic
kidney disease presents with a progressively worsening headache over several months that has not
responded to acetaminophen. A review of systems is unremarkable. On examination, his blood
pressure is 135/87 mm Hg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, temperature is 36.7°C, and oxygen
saturation is 99% on room air. Visual-field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopsia. Cardiac
examination shows a regular rhythm, lung auscultation is clear, and there is trace edema in the lower
extremities. Extraocular movements are intact, and the neurologic exam is otherwise normal.
Laboratory results indicate normal electrolytes, a serum creatinine level of 1.74 mg/dL (0.8–1.3), an
estimated glomerular filtration rate of 45 mL/min/1.73 m² (≥60), a hemoglobin level of 13.2 g/dL
(13.5–17.5), and normal leukocyte and platelet counts. Which imaging modality is the most appropriate
to evaluate this patient? Answer Choices: (A) Digital subtraction angiography (B) CT with iodinated
contrast (C) MRI with gadolinium (D) CT without iodinated contrast (E) MRI without gadolinium (F)
SPECT imaging (G) Cerebral angiography (H) PET-CT scan (I) MR venography without contrast (J) CT
angiography
 A. Cerebral angiography
B. CT without iodinated contrast
C. SPECT imaging
D. PET-CT scan
E. MRI with gadolinium
F. CT angiography
G. CT with iodinated contrast
H. Digital subtraction angiography
I. MRI without gadolinium
J. MR venography without contrast
